title: Does Eating Organic Make You Healthier?

sentences.text: Picture a pair of shoppers: the first fills the cart with organic food, the other buys whatever is cheapest.
Years later, the organic shopper is in better health.
sentences.note: Plainly hypothetical, no figure; s08 shows observational studies do find organic eaters with lower rates of several conditions, and s09 qualifies it.

sentences.text: Was it the food, or the kind of person who buys it?
And behind that sits a second question: does organic food lower your risk of cancer?

sections.name: question-1
sections.title: Does eating organic make you healthier?

sentences.text: The channel Seeker makes one case: "it seems to me that organic has lots of health benefits".

assertions.text: Seeker said it seems to its presenter that organic has lots of health benefits.

quote.text: it seems to me that organic has lots of health benefits
quote.speaker: Seeker

sentences.text: Dr. Jason West goes further, saying eating organic "helps to prevent autoimmune and chronic diseases".

assertions.text: Dr. Jason West said eating organic helps to prevent autoimmune and chronic diseases.

quote.text: helps to prevent autoimmune and chronic diseases
quote.speaker: Dr. Jason West

sentences.text: Harvard Health disagrees: "there isn’t clear evidence that organic foods are also healthier for people".

assertions.text: Harvard Health wrote that there isn't clear evidence that organic foods are also healthier for people.

quote.text: there isn’t clear evidence that organic foods are also healthier for people
quote.speaker: Harvard Health

sentences.text: A systematic review found that, in observational studies, eating organic went along with lower rates of metabolic syndrome, high body weight, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, infertility and birth defects, among other outcomes.
sentences.note: The review's own list (L135); s09 gives its warning that diet and lifestyle likely sway these results, and s17 its conclusion that no long-term benefit can be stated.

assertions.text: The Vigar systematic review reports significant positive outcomes from observational studies, including reduced incidence of metabolic syndrome, high BMI, non-Hodgkin lymphoma, infertility and birth defects, while the evidence base does not allow a definitive statement of long-term benefit.
qualifications: s08 says these are observational studies; s09 gives the review's warning about diet and lifestyle.

sentences.text: The same review warns that organic eating often comes with a healthier diet overall and less overweight, and that this is likely to sway those results.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says organic food consumption is often tied to healthier dietary practices and lower levels of overweight and obesity, which are likely to be influential in the results of observational research.

sentences.text: A second review saw similar signals, for childhood allergies, adult overweight and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and concluded that it is not yet possible to say whether organic food causes any of them.

assertions.text: The Mie review reports indications of lower childhood allergies, adult overweight/obesity and non-Hodgkin lymphoma in organic consumers, and says it is presently not possible to determine whether organic food plays a causal role.

sentences.text: Its authors point out that people who prefer organic also eat more fruit, vegetables, whole grains and legumes and less meat, and they expect those people to have less diabetes and cardiovascular disease as a consequence of that diet.

assertions.text: The Mie review says consumers who prefer organic food eat more fruit, vegetables, whole grains and legumes and less meat, and expects them to have a decreased risk of diabetes and cardiovascular disease as a consequence of these dietary patterns.

sentences.text: What about trials, where researchers change what people eat and watch what happens?
Those trials have been short, and have mostly measured stand-in markers rather than disease itself, with limited positive results.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says clinical trial research has been short-term and measured largely surrogate markers with limited positive results.

sentences.text: Another review counted 17 studies in people, and only 3 of them looked at actual illness: they found no significant differences in allergic conditions or in symptomatic Campylobacter infection.

assertions.text: The Smith-Spangler review included 17 human studies; only 3 examined clinical outcomes, finding no significant differences for allergic outcomes or symptomatic Campylobacter infection.
qualifications: s14 presents it as one review ("Another review") and names how few human studies looked at illness.

sentences.text: Studies in adults that measured nutrients and other markers in blood, urine, breast milk and semen found no clinically meaningful differences.

assertions.text: The Smith-Spangler review reports that studies of biomarker and nutrient levels in serum, urine, breast milk and semen in adults did not identify clinically meaningful differences.
qualifications: s15 continues the same single review, limited to adults and to biomarker studies.

sentences.text: And a report on organic foods found no well-powered human study that directly shows a health benefit, or protection from disease, from eating an organic diet.

assertions.text: The AAP report says there are no well-powered human studies that directly demonstrate health benefits or disease protection from consuming an organic diet.
qualifications: s16 presents it as one report and keeps its wording (well-powered, directly).

sentences.text: So no health benefit of eating organic has been proven in the people who eat it.

assertions.text: The reviews find that the evidence does not allow a definitive statement on long-term health benefits of organic food, and no well-powered human study demonstrates one.

sentences.text: Not proven is not the same as ruled out: studies consistently find fewer pesticide breakdown products in the urine of people on an organic diet, and the first review's authors think it possible that lower exposure, kept up over time, could turn into health benefits.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says pesticide excretion studies have consistently shown a reduction in urinary pesticide metabolites with an organic diet, but there is insufficient evidence that this translates into clinically meaningful health outcomes.
The Vigar review says it seems possible that ongoing reduced pesticide exposure may translate to health benefits.

sentences.text: If a benefit is there, could it show up in the outcome people fear most: who gets cancer?

sections.name: question-2
sections.title: Does eating organic lower your risk of cancer?

sentences.text: Tim Spector, on the ZOE channel, says one study found "the organic food group were protected by about 25 percent".

assertions.text: Tim Spector said that in one study the organic food group were protected by about 25 percent against cancer.

quote.text: the organic food group were protected by about 25 percent
quote.speaker: Tim Spector

sentences.text: A Dana-Farber Cancer Institute video describes a large study of British women that found "organic food intake was not associated with a decreased cancer risk for the cancers that they evaluated".

assertions.text: A Dana-Farber Cancer Institute video said a large study of UK women found organic food intake was not associated with a decreased cancer risk for the cancers evaluated.

quote.text: organic food intake was not associated with a decreased cancer risk for the cancers that they evaluated
quote.speaker: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute

sentences.text: The NutriNet-Santé cohort followed 68,946 adults for an average of 4.6 years, and after adjusting for other factors, the quarter who scored highest for eating organic had a 25 percent lower rate of cancer than the quarter who scored lowest.

assertions.text: NutriNet-Santé followed 68,946 participants for a mean of 4.6 years; after adjustment for confounders, the top quartile of organic food score had a hazard ratio of 0.75 for overall cancer against the bottom quartile, a 25 percent lower hazard.
qualifications: s23 gives the absolute difference of 0.6 percent; s30 and s32 say the high organic eaters also differed in income, education, activity and diet, which the observational design cannot separate.

sentences.text: In absolute terms, though, the difference in the share of people who got cancer was 0.6 percent.

assertions.text: NutriNet-Santé reports an absolute risk reduction of 0.6% for the top against the bottom quartile of organic food score.
qualifications: s23 itself carries the absolute size of the hazard reduction in s22.

sentences.text: The lower risk showed up for non-Hodgkin lymphoma and postmenopausal breast cancer, and not for other types of cancer.

assertions.text: Among specific cancers, NutriNet-Santé found a decreased risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma and postmenopausal breast cancer, with no association for other types of cancer.
qualifications: s24 narrows the overall association to two cancers and none for the rest.

sentences.text: In the United Kingdom, the Million Women Study followed its participants for about 9 years.

assertions.text: The Million Women Study in the United Kingdom examined organic diet and cancer over a 9-year follow-up.
qualifications: s26 and s27 give what this cohort found, with its self-reported intake and the hedged lymphoma result.

sentences.text: Women who said they usually or always ate organic had no lower rate of cancer overall than women who said they never did, and a slightly higher rate of breast cancer.

assertions.text: In the Million Women Study, self-reported usually/always organic consumption against never was not associated with a reduction in all cancer (RR 1.03, CI 0.99-1.07) and was associated with slightly higher breast cancer (RR 1.09, CI 1.02-1.15).

sentences.text: The one cancer that was lower was non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and the authors' conclusion hedges even that: "except possibly for non-Hodgkin lymphoma".

assertions.text: The Million Women Study found organic consumption associated with lower non-Hodgkin lymphoma (RR 0.79) and concluded there was little or no decrease in cancer except possibly for non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

sentences.text: So these cohorts agree on lymphoma and point in opposite directions on breast cancer.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says the NutriNet-Santé finding on non-Hodgkin lymphoma is similar to the Million Women Study's, while the finding on breast cancer is in direct contrast.
qualifications: s28 reports the one signal the two cohorts share alongside the one where they conflict.

sentences.text: Why would the cohorts disagree?

In NutriNet-Santé, the higher people scored for eating organic, the more likely they were to be women, better paid, better educated and physically active, and the more fruit, vegetables, nuts and legumes and the less meat they ate.

assertions.text: In NutriNet-Santé, higher organic food scores were associated with female sex, high occupational status or income, postsecondary education and physical activity, and with higher intake of fruits, vegetables, nuts and legumes and lower intake of processed meat, other meat and poultry.
qualifications: s31 says the socioeconomic differences were smaller in the UK cohort.

sentences.text: In the British study, women who usually or always ate organic were more likely to report strenuous exercise and less likely to smoke or eat red and processed meat, though differences in socioeconomic status were smaller.

assertions.text: In the Million Women Study, women who usually or always ate organic were more likely to report strenuous physical activity and less likely to smoke or eat red and processed meat, with smaller differences in socioeconomic status.
qualifications: s31 itself says the socioeconomic differences were smaller.

sentences.text: The French team found that adding more diet measures did not change its result, but the systematic review from earlier notes that studies adjust for diet in different ways, so a benefit may still be partly down to whole-food diets and healthier lives rather than the organic food itself.

assertions.text: NutriNet-Santé reports that accounting for other additional dietary factors did not modify its finding on organic food score and overall cancer risk.
qualifications: The same sentence gives the systematic review's caveat that a benefit may still be partly due to diet and lifestyle; s33 states the small absolute difference.

assertions.text: The Vigar review says diet quality has been measured and adjusted for in different ways in observational research, and that any benefits from organic food consumption may be attributable partly to increased wholefood intake and a healthier lifestyle, rather than a direct effect of organic food.
qualifications: s31 says socioeconomic differences were smaller in the UK cohort; s32 says partly, not wholly.

sentences.text: So the evidence does not show that organic food lowers cancer risk: one cohort found no overall drop, and the other found a small absolute difference among people who also ate and lived differently.

assertions.text: The Million Women Study found no reduction in all cancer with organic food, and NutriNet-Santé found an absolute risk reduction of 0.6% in its top organic quartile, so organic food has not been shown to lower cancer risk.
qualifications: s33 itself names the small absolute difference and the lifestyle differences in the cohort that found it.

assertions.text: High organic consumers in NutriNet-Santé also differed in diet and lifestyle, which may account for part of any benefit.
qualifications: s31 says income differed less in the UK cohort.

sentences.text: So the next time a label or a video promises that organic food will keep you well, ask one question: was the benefit measured in people who were given the food, or in people who chose it?
Then ask what was counted, an illness or a number on a blood test, and for how long.
